title: Whither shall I flee?
hook: if I take the wings of the morning, even there (Psalm 139)
tomorrow: a psalm with wild goats, lions and a sea monster at play. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday: lift up mine eyes, to the hills and past them, to a keeper who doesn't sleep. That keeper was watching the road. Today, someone tries to leave it.
screen: `LIFT UP MINE EYES.` → `SOMEONE LEAVES THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Jonah gets a call from God to go to Nineveh, and he goes down to the port instead. The book of Jonah says he rose up "to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD," and paid the fare, as if God's presence stopped at the dock. Then a storm, a crew throwing cargo overboard, Jonah thrown into the sea, and a great fish. And from inside the fish, Jonah prays. So what was waiting at the edge of the map? The one he ran from. Psalm 139 has an odd way of saying that: it lists hiding places like someone checking every exit.
screen: `A TICKET TO TARSHISH.` → `A STORM, A SEA, A FISH.` → `EVERY EXIT, CHECKED.`

segments.voice: The psalm asks, "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Then the list. "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." Hell here is the Hebrew Sheol, the place of the dead. Up as far as up goes, down as far as down goes. Then across: "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." Here's the puzzle. Read cold, this sounds like surveillance: nowhere to hide. But look at the hand at the end of the list. It doesn't grab; it leads and holds. And the psalm opens, "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." Known all the way down, and held anyway. That's the teaching Jews and Christians draw from it: God is present everywhere, so no ship, no sea and no grave is out of reach. Jonah learned it the hard way. One to tell a friend: Jewish tradition reads the book of Jonah on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, a story about a man who couldn't outrun God, read on the day people come back. And the psalm's own answer to its puzzle is a few lines on: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."
screen: `WHITHER SHALL I FLEE?` · `HEAVEN, SHEOL, THE FAR SEA.` · `A HAND THAT LEADS AND HOLDS.` · `JONAH, READ ON YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `WINGS OF THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and sit as you are, not as you'd like to be seen. Let one true thing about today come to mind, a worry or a mistake, and don't fix it. Just let it be fully known, and keep breathing.
Whither shall I flee? The psalm's question with no exit: not heaven, not Sheol, not the far sea, and a hand there to hold.
Hold on to this: the wings of the morning still land in a hand that holds. The hills yesterday, the far sea today: this psalm travels too.

howItsDone: Psalm 139 is prayed by Jews and Christians as a psalm of being known by God; in synagogues the book of Jonah is read on the afternoon of Yom Kippur.

fork.setup: your friend's grandmother is moving into a care home far from her old church, and she's afraid God won't find her there. what would Psalm 139 say?
options: there's no place too far: even there shall thy hand lead me.
she'll be fine as soon as she finds a new church nearby.
it says no one can hide from God's judgment, wherever they go.
fork.reveal: the psalm's list of far places ends in a hand that leads and holds, at the uttermost parts of the sea.

original.note: Hebrew, Psalm 139:9: wings of the dawn, the KJV's wings of the morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary line: you can't hide from God.
what it means: you can't fall out of reach: heaven, Sheol or the far sea, the hand still leads and holds.
what a scholar hears: Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead in the Hebrew Bible; and the opening, thou hast searched me, and known me, frames the whole list.
guess: a psalm's question: where could I go to get away from God?
a prophet's plea to be taken off a sinking ship
a soldier's prayer before running from a lost battle

chat.says: no callbacks. honestly part of me wants to move somewhere nobody knows me and start over
options: Maybe move someday, but not to escape. Psalm 139 says even the far sea isn't out of reach.
Go! That's the psalm's point: take the wings of the morning and start completely fresh.
Never move. Jonah ran from God and got swallowed; leaving is always running away.
chat.meaning: In Psalm 139 there's nowhere to flee: heaven, Sheol, the far sea. Jonah tried. A new city is fine; being known comes along.

tie.story: Jonah paid the fare to flee from the presence of the LORD, and was met at the bottom of the sea.
tie.friend: Zoe can choose a move for its own sake someday, knowing she'd bring the same self along.
tie.you: is there anything you're trying to outrun?
